𝐎𝐧 𝐕𝐢𝐞𝐰 | 𝐉𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐥 𝐁𝐞𝐧 𝐀𝐛𝐝𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐡

Jellal Ben Abdallah built a singular pictorial world where tradition meets modernity. Rooted in the spirit of Sidi Bou Saïd, his practice transforms everyday life, traditional crafts, and intimate interiors into refined visual poetry. Delicate color, fine hieratic line, and simplified form define a language both intimate and monumental—extending from miniature painting to public fresco and stage decoration. Celebrating Tunisian heritage while embracing a contemporary artistic vocabulary, his work holds memory and innovation in timeless balance.

ocr:
Jellal Ben Abdallah
Painter of Tunisian memory — between miniature and
modernity
Jellal Ben Abdallah chose painting in 1938, inspired by
Sidi Bou Saïd. He began with Oriental miniatures, later
engaging with the School of Tunis. His work Le Martyr,
after the April 1938 events, marked his engaged debut.
After losing his grandmother and parents, he settled
permanently in Sidi Bou Saïd. In 1943, he exhibited his
first large miniatures. Though enrolled at the École des
Beaux-Arts de Tunis for only three weeks, he won the
First Prize for painting, funding a Paris stay. He studied
at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière, then joined
Moses Levy in Rome.
In 1951, he received his first major public commission:
frescoes for a girls’ high school in Sousse. The Tunisian
State later commissioned work for the Maison de Tunisie
in Paris, where he lived two years. The Champion-Cordier
gallery distributed his work internationally.
In 1957, he became decorator of the Théâtre municipal
de Tunis for thirteen years. His last major exhibition was
in 1997. His style features fine, hieratic drawing, delicate
colors, and a blend of tradition and modernity.

𝐎𝐧 𝐕𝐢𝐞𝐰 | 𝐁𝐫𝐚𝐡𝐢𝐦 𝐃𝐡𝐚𝐡𝐚𝐤

A self-taught painter and printmaker of the School of Tunis, Dhahak occupies a singular position: formed between Tunisian tradition and European modernism. 
His Roman training (1957–61) under Amerigo Bartoli and Macari proved decisive, culminating in the Carlo Giviera Prize. Returning to Tunisia, he asserted artistic independence after teaching in Sfax. From his first Tunis solo show (1964) to the Cité des Arts, Paris (1972), and his Sidi Bou Saïd printmaking studio, his practice unites technical rigor with a profoundly Mediterranean sensitivity—recognized by the Grand Prix de Tunis (1991) and the National Prize for Plastic Arts (1994).

ocr:
Brahim Dhahak
Self-taught painter and printmaker — between
Tunis, Rome, and Paris
A self-taught painter and member of the School of
Tunis, he attended Rome's Artistic Academy from
1957 to 1961, a decisive period that transformed
him into an accomplished master. Studying under
Amerigo Bartoli and master printmaker Macari, he
refined his technique and won the Carlo Giviera
Prize in 1961.
Returning to Tunisia at 30, he taught drawing
in Sfax. Shorty after, he left to preserve his
independence. His first solo exhibition was held in
Tunis in 1964, before a stay at the Cité des Arts in
Paris in 1972. From then on, he exhibited regularly
in Tunisia and abroad, in the context of solo and
group exhibitions.
An accomplished printmaker, he produced an
important body of work in this field in his studio in
Sidi Bou Said. His creations earned him the Grand
Prix of the City of Tunis in 1991, and then the
National Prize for Plastic Arts in 1994.
Brahim Dhahak embodies the image of a complete
artist, nourished by the dialogue between
Tunisian tradition and European know-how,
whose technical rigor is allied with a profoundly
Mediterranean sensitivity.
